sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Sepsis Workup
sections.description: This section covers the patient's initial emergency department presentation, including the dog bite history, the development of septic shock with DIC, the key laboratory derangements, and the clinical reasoning that led to early suspicion of Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage. It establishes the clinical foundation upon which the later diagnostic pivot to TMA is built.
subtopics: History: Dog bite to upper lip, delayed antibiotic initiation, tetanus prophylaxis
Presenting symptoms: High fever, mottled lower extremities, refractory hypoglycemia, septic appearance
Initial laboratory derangements: Pancytopenia, coagulopathy, AKI, liver enzyme elevation, metabolic acidosis, hyperlactatemia
Clinical reasoning for sepsis with DIC: qSOFA score, ruling out necrotizing fasciitis
Empiric antibiotic strategy: Piperacillin/tazobactam to cover dog-associated pathogens including Capnocytophaga
Early suspicion and eventual blood culture confirmation of C. canimorsus bacteraemia
Initial management: ICU transfer, fluid resuscitation, blood product support, stress-dose corticosteroids

sections.section_title: Capnocytophaga canimorsus: Pathogen Biology and Infection Spectrum
sections.description: This section provides the microbiological and clinical background on C. canimorsus necessary to understand the case, covering its habitat, modes of transmission, the wide spectrum of clinical disease in humans, diagnostic challenges related to its fastidious growth, and its broad antibiotic susceptibility profile.
subtopics: Microbiological characteristics: Slow-growing, encapsulated, gram-negative rod
Habitat and transmission: Normal oropharyngeal flora of dogs and cats; transmission via bites, scratches, close contact
Spectrum of human disease: From isolated meningitis to fulminant sepsis, DIC, multiorgan failure, and TMA
Mortality approaching 30% despite broad antibiotic susceptibility
Diagnostic challenges: Fastidious nature, slow culture growth, increasing role of molecular methods such as real-time nanopore sequencing
Clinical context: Why dog bite history is a critical clue for empiric antibiotic coverage

sections.section_title: Clinical Evolution: From Resolving Sepsis to Thrombotic Microangiopathy
sections.description: This section traces the patient's clinical course from the ICU through the nephrology ward, detailing the development of anuria and dialysis dependence, microthrombotic complications, the initial clinical improvement with antibiotic therapy, and the critical turning point when sudden isolated hemolysis and persistent thrombocytopenia signaled a superimposed thrombotic microangiopathy that could not be explained by ongoing sepsis or DIC alone.
subtopics: ICU course: Complete anuria, septic cardiomyopathy, initiation of continuous renal replacement therapy
Microthrombotic phenomena: Diffuse ecchymoses, distal cyanotic and ischaemic changes in digits and toes
Transfer to nephrology ward: Dialysis-dependent AKI, antibiotic de-escalation based on culture results, initial clinical and laboratory improvement
The diagnostic turning point: Sudden isolated hemoglobin drop (111 to 68 g/L) without evidence of bleeding
Laboratory evidence of ongoing hemolysis: Undetectable haptoglobin, rising LDH, persistent thrombocytopenia
False-positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT): Initially attributed to autoimmune hemolytic anemia; role of penicillin and prior transfusions in false positivity; repeat testing negative
Peripheral blood smear revealing 15-20% schistocytes: Recognition of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) and suspicion of TMA

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis of TMA: A Systematic Diagnostic Approach
sections.description: This section outlines the structured framework for differentiating the major thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes—TTP, STEC-HUS, and CM-HUS—using clinical prediction scores, laboratory assays, microbiological testing, and renal biopsy findings, demonstrating how each alternative was systematically excluded or confirmed in this patient.
subtopics: TMA as an umbrella syndrome: The triad of MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and organ damage
Excluding thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP): PLASMIC score (4/7, low probability), ADAMTS13 activity at 43.5% (TTP requires <10%)
Excluding Shiga toxin-producing E. coli HUS (STEC-HUS): Negative stool PCR, absence of prodromal diarrheal illness
Complement studies: C3 and C4 may be normal in CM-HUS; extended testing including alternative pathway AH50 assay
Role and findings of renal biopsy: Severe acute tubular necrosis, ischaemic glomeruli with fibrin thrombi, scattered crescent formation
CM-HUS as a clinicopathological diagnosis of exclusion
Critical importance of timing of complement testing relative to plasma exchange and eculizumab administration

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology of CM-HUS: Complement Dysregulation and Infectious Triggers
sections.description: This section explains the mechanisms underlying complement-mediated HUS, including alternative pathway dysregulation, the role of genetic predisposition and incomplete penetrance, the two-hit model of disease, and how C. canimorsus infection can serve as a trigger. It also addresses the unique finding in this case of no demonstrable inherited complement defect.
subtopics: Alternative complement pathway and its regulation by factors H, I, B, and membrane cofactor protein (CD46)
Genetic variants and autoantibodies found in 50-70% of CM-HUS patients
Incomplete disease penetrance: The concept that an external trigger is typically required for clinical manifestation
The two-hit model: Genetic predisposition plus environmental trigger such as infection, pregnancy, or medications
How infections activate the complement system and may unmask latent complement dysregulation
C. canimorsus and complement: Variable serum susceptibility, capsule-mediated partial resistance, and the clinical paradox of complement-driven pathogen clearance versus endothelial damage
This case versus previously reported cases: No pathogenic complement gene variants identified, supporting infection-triggered CM-HUS without demonstrable inherited predisposition

sections.section_title: Treatment Strategy, Clinical Dilemmas, and Outcome
sections.description: This section covers the therapeutic approach to CM-HUS in the context of recent C. canimorsus sepsis, including the rationale and limitations of plasma exchange as bridging therapy, eculizumab mechanism and dosing, the infectious risk management with vaccination and prophylaxis, and the patient's clinical outcome and follow-up. It also addresses broader clinical implications for recognizing infection-triggered CM-HUS.
subtopics: Plasma exchange (PEX) as bridging therapy: Removing circulating complement fragments and inflammatory mediators; transient benefit in CM-HUS versus lifesaving role in TTP
Eculizumab: Anti-C5 monoclonal antibody, mechanism of terminal complement blockade, induction (900 mg weekly for 4 weeks) and maintenance (1200 mg every 2 weeks) dosing
The therapeutic dilemma of complement blockade during or after active bacteraemia: Risk of uncontrolled infection with encapsulated organisms
Vaccination strategy before eculizumab: Meningococcal vaccines (Menveo and Bexsero), timing considerations
Antibiotic prophylaxis during complement blockade: Penicillin prophylaxis when vaccines were not administered 2 weeks prior
Timing of eculizumab initiation after blood cultures became negative
Clinical outcome: Hematological remission, partial renal recovery (creatinine 175 µmol/L), return of urine output after PEX and sustained improvement after eculizumab
Prognostic determinants: Time-to-eculizumab initiation and baseline renal function
Reassessment for potential discontinuation: Role of genetic testing results in guiding duration of complement blockade
